title: Canonical splice sites of human lncRNA genes, including 22,213 added from long-read data, show no depletion of rare variants in 76,215 genomes (chromosomes 1, 10, 11 and part of 12)
abstract: In 76,215 human genomes, the splice sites of long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) genes carry as many rare variants as expected, unlike the splice sites of protein-coding genes. This matters because GENCODE release 47 almost doubled the annotated lncRNA genes with models from long-read sequencing, and it is not known how many of these spliced transcripts have a function. A splice site needs its canonical bases (GT at the intron start, AG at the end) only if the spliced RNA, or splicing itself, is useful; selection then removes mutations there, so fewer variants occur than the mutation rate predicts (depletion). We counted single-nucleotide variants (gnomAD v4.1) at the GT/AG bases of 38,650 lncRNA splice sites (5,722 genes) on chromosomes 1, 10, 11 and part of 12, against a strand-specific sequence-context model calibrated on intron bases 41-120 bp from the same junctions. Depletion was 54.3% (95% CI 51.5 to 56.9) at protein-coding splice sites, 22.6% (18.1 to 27.1) at untranslated-region (UTR) introns, and -0.2% (-2.3 to 1.7) at lncRNA sites; for rare variants (frequency below 1e-4), -0.9% (-3.1 to 1.3). Sites first annotated in release 47 (22,213) and older manually annotated sites did not differ (0.4% and 0.9%). No group had a clear rare-variant depletion, including junctions used in 1,000 or more GTEx samples (0.7%) and sites conserved in 241 mammals (7.9%, -1.0 to 17.4). Statistically, at most 2.5% of lncRNA sites can be under selection as strong as at coding splice sites and 6.9% as strong as at UTR introns; with a 4-point allowance for systematic error (single canonical bases differ by about 4 points) the limits are about 10% and 28%. Exploratory: at well-used junctions (15% of sites), variants with frequency 1e-3 to 1e-2 were depleted 31% (5 to 55), against 1% elsewhere, and the depletion grew with frequency, also for alleles common only in African-ancestry genomes: the pattern of weak purifying selection. Variants with frequency 1e-2 or more were depleted at all junction groups (18-39%), which a bias in junction discovery can partly explain. Limits: 4 of 22 autosomes were analysed because the shared network failed; the test sees only selection on splicing in heterozygotes, not other functions of lncRNA loci.

display.caption: Depletion of variant alleles (1 - observed/expected) at canonical GT/AG splice bases in 76,215 gnomAD genomes, chromosomes 1, 10, 11 and part of 12. A: all alleles; B: rare alleles (AF < 1e-4). Protein-coding splice sites lose about half of the expected alleles; lncRNA splice sites, old or new, lose none. Lines: 95% bootstrap intervals over genes, with context-model error.

A: rare-allele depletion at lncRNA splice sites by GTEx junction use, gene expression, mammalian conservation and transposable-element origin; none approaches coding or UTR-intron levels (dashed lines). B: depletion by allele frequency. lncRNA junctions used in 1,000 or more GTEx samples show depletion that grows with frequency from 1e-3 (weak selection); junctions new in GENCODE v47 show depletion only at AF >= 1e-2.
Depletion along the splice region (non-CpG bases). Coding exon ends and intron bases 3-6 are constrained; lncRNA bases are not constrained at any position.

Dukler et al. 2022 (ExtRaINSIGHT, gnomAD v3) estimated a very small strongly selected fraction for lncRNA exons; our site-level test of lncRNA canonical splice sites, including the GENCODE v47 long-read junctions, agrees and refines it.
GENCODE v47 annotation (with v46 and v50) defines the splice sites and their classes.
GENCODE reference annotation.

The CLS preprint reports that the new long-read lncRNA annotations display evolutionary constraints (phyloP); in 76,215 human genomes their canonical splice sites show no depletion of rare variants (0.4%, -2.0 to 3.0). The measures differ (mammalian conservation versus present-day selection).

Used splice-site conservation to argue that most lncRNAs are well conserved; present-day human variation shows no rare-variant depletion at lncRNA splice sites, and only a non-significant 7.9% at mammal-conserved ones.
Reported that lincRNA constraint concentrates at exon ends; gnomAD shows no depletion at lncRNA exon-end bases, although the method detects only about 6% even at UTR exon ends.
Reported selection on splicing enhancers in multiexonic lncRNA exons; we find no present-day depletion at exon ends or splice sites.
Reported that lncRNA mutations are effectively neutral in humans; we find the same for lncRNA splice sites with much larger data.
Proposes that most lncRNA transcript models reflect noise; consistent with absent selection at their splice sites.
Universal alternative splicing of non-coding exons; consistent with unconstrained lncRNA splicing.
Drift limits splicing accuracy; low-abundance isoforms are mostly errors.
Reports less precise splice-site selection in lncRNAs.
lncRNA loci can act through promoters, transcription and splicing in cis; our test covers only the splicing part.
